# `Cargo.lock` — the dependency lockfile

Generated by Cargo after the first `cargo build` / `cargo run` / `cargo test`. Even with zero dependencies, Cargo creates one:

```toml
# This file is automatically @generated by Cargo.
# It is not intended for manual editing.
version = 4

[[package]]
name = "cawir"
version = "0.1.0"
```

## Cargo.toml vs Cargo.lock

| | `Cargo.toml` | `Cargo.lock` |
|---|---|---|
| Written by | You (manually or via `cargo add`) | Cargo (automatically) |
| Contains | **Requirements** — "I want `reqwest = "0.12"`" | **Resolutions** — "last time I resolved that, it landed on `reqwest 0.12.9`, with these exact transitive deps, with these exact SHA256 checksums — use those" |
| Purpose | Declare intent | Guarantee reproducibility |
| Human-readable? | Yes, you write it | Generated — don't edit by hand |

When you add a dep to `Cargo.toml`, Cargo's resolver picks concrete versions that satisfy your constraints, writes them to `Cargo.lock`, and downloads them. Next time anyone builds the project, Cargo consults the lockfile first — so every machine gets the same versions.

## Binary vs library — should you commit it?

This is the one policy decision that matters:

| Crate type | Commit `Cargo.lock`? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Binary** | ✅ Yes | You want reproducible builds. Every `cargo build` on any machine resolves to the same exact dep versions. |
| **Library** | ❌ No, `.gitignore` it | You want downstream users to resolve their own dep versions against their own constraints. Pinning your own lockfile would have no effect on them, and can cause confusion. |

cawir is a binary (see `03a-cargo-cli-and-crate-types.md`), so it's committed.

### Why libraries skip it

If you publish a library to crates.io, downstream users depend on it via *their* `Cargo.toml`. *Their* `Cargo.lock` is what controls their build. Your library's lockfile is unused in their build. Keeping it in your repo just adds noise and potential merge conflicts.

## Ecosystem comparison

| Ecosystem | Lockfile | Typical git policy |
|---|---|---|
| Rust binary | `Cargo.lock` | commit |
| Rust library | `Cargo.lock` | gitignore |
| Node | `package-lock.json` / `yarn.lock` / `pnpm-lock.yaml` | commit |
| Python (Poetry / uv) | `poetry.lock` / `uv.lock` | commit |
| Go | `go.sum` | commit |
| Ruby | `Gemfile.lock` | commit for apps, ignore for gems (libraries) |

The Rust binary-vs-library split matches the Ruby app-vs-gem split — same underlying reasoning.

## When does the lockfile update?

- `cargo add <crate>` — resolver runs, updates `Cargo.toml` AND `Cargo.lock`
- `cargo update` — re-resolves all deps to their latest-allowed versions (`Cargo.toml` untouched)
- `cargo update -p <crate>` — re-resolves just one dep
- First `cargo build` / `run` / `test` in a fresh clone — reads the lockfile, downloads the pinned versions
- If `Cargo.toml` is edited in a way the lockfile can still satisfy, the lockfile may be partially amended automatically

## Do NOT edit by hand

`Cargo.lock` is generated; manual edits will be silently overwritten on the next resolver run. If you need to force a specific version, set the constraint in `Cargo.toml`, then `cargo update`.
